name: Sprint/HIIT for growth hormone

lead: Some teenagers do all-out sprints or interval workouts because intense exercise triggers a growth hormone (GH) surge, and GH is the hormone most associated with childhood growth. The hope is that more GH signalling during puberty adds height.

Vigorous exercise is a recognised stimulus of GH pulses, and GH acts on growth cartilage directly and through IGF-1 from the liver. The exercise-GH link is documented, but reference sources do not state that exercise-triggered pulses change final adult height, and no published trial has tested sprint or HIIT training for adult height.

paras: People add sprint sessions or interval circuits to their weekly training during adolescence, often alongside sleep and nutrition habits they also link to growth. The workouts double as general conditioning and leanness work.

Sprint and interval training carry the usual risks of high-intensity exercise, such as muscle and tendon strain. Adult height is described as largely genetic, with nutrition and health as the main modifiable factors.

angle.text: Teens do sprints and HIIT because vigorous exercise briefly raises growth hormone, and they hope that extra signalling supports more growth. The short-term GH rise is documented; a link to final height has not been tested in trials.

lead: Sprint or high-intensity interval training (HIIT) for growth hormone is a height-related practice in which teenagers do all-out sprints or interval workouts in the belief that the resulting surge in growth hormone (GH) will help them grow taller or look more developed. It rests on the fact that vigorous exercise is a recognised stimulus of GH secretion, and GH is the hormone best known for its role in childhood growth.

Wikipedia describes increased childhood height as GH's most widely known effect, working both directly on cartilage cells and through IGF-1 made mainly in the liver, and notes that young adolescents secrete roughly 700 micrograms a day versus about 400 in healthy adults. HIIT itself alternates short, intense efforts with brief recoveries, and the same encyclopedia entry reports that in adolescents it can increase muscle mass, especially in the mid-to-late teens, and can reduce body fat in youth with obesity. For appearance, that gives the practice a second payoff alongside the height hope: a leaner, more muscular build.

Small studies of sprint exercise confirm that GH rises after a single maximal effort and stays elevated for one to two hours, and that the rise is larger for 30-second sprints than for 6-second ones.[1] Adult height is described as largely heritable, with nutrition and health in childhood the main environmental factors, and no published trial has tested sprint or HIIT training as a way to change final height in healthy adolescents.

paras: Practitioners describe short, maximal-effort sprints, hill sprints or interval circuits performed several times a week, sometimes combined with sleep and nutrition routines, with the stated aim of maximising natural GH release during the years when growth is still possible.

HIIT is a training format with a warm-up, intense intervals separated by easier recovery, and a cool-down. Wikipedia reports sessions typically run under 30 minutes, intervals usually last 20 to 45 seconds, and a common ratio is about 2:1 work to rest, though there is no single formula. Sprint interval training (SIT) is a variant using supramaximal all-out efforts in shorter bursts with lower total volume and longer recovery.

sections.h: How people use it for their looks
paras: For height, teenagers and parents who follow height-growth forums add sprinting to routines alongside sleep, nutrition and stretching, reasoning that a GH pulse during puberty can only help. For physique, interval work is used as a time-efficient way to lose fat and build athletic conditioning; a T Nation thread asks whether high-intensity training helps fat loss, reflecting the same interest in lean, defined appearance.[2]
Sprint sessions are commonly done on a track, hill, bike or treadmill. Because the GH response depends on the effort, practitioners aim for truly maximal bursts rather than steady jogging.[1]

The method is often traced to Peter Coe, who in the 1970s had his son Sebastian Coe repeat fast 200 metre runs with short recoveries. In 1996 Izumi Tabata of Ritsumeikan University and colleagues studied Olympic speed skaters on 20 seconds of very hard effort followed by 10 seconds of rest repeated for 8 cycles; over 6 weeks it matched the aerobic gains of a steady-state group while adding anaerobic capacity. Martin Gibala of McMaster University popularised a 60-seconds-hard, 75-seconds-easy cycling format in 2010, and Vollaard later proposed a protocol of two 20-second all-out sprints.

Doping and sports-medicine history adds context: athletes have used synthetic GH since at least 1982, and recombinant GH was FDA-approved in 1985, which is part of why GH has become a cultural shorthand for growth and physique.

GH is released in pulses. Wikipedia lists sleep, vigorous exercise, fasting, sex hormones in puberty and ghrelin among stimulators, describes the largest daily peak as occurring about an hour after sleep onset, and notes that sleep deprivation suppresses release. In children, GH deficiency causes growth failure and short stature, which underlies the idea that more GH could mean more height; recombinant GH is used for childhood growth disorders and other conditions under medical supervision.

Twin studies cited by Wikipedia estimate that 60 to 80 percent of height variation within a population is heritable, and growth reaches zero on average around 15 to 16 in females and 18 to 19 in males. Epiphyseal (growth) plates fuse as early as 12 in girls and 14 in boys, most commonly at 14 to 15 and 15 to 17 respectively, and rising estrogen during puberty reduces growth-plate cartilage activity until growth stops.[3] Chronic malnutrition during childhood is associated with reduced adult height.

In a within-subject study of nine men, a single 30-second maximal cycle sprint produced a peak mean GH more than 450 percent higher than a 6-second sprint and kept GH elevated for 90 to 120 minutes, compared with about 60 minutes after the shorter sprint; there was large variation between individuals, and GH did not rise in a no-exercise control trial.[1]

In 27 non-obese men aged 18 to 32, GH rose after a 30-second sprint and age was a significant negative predictor of the response, while sprint performance and BMI were not.[1] Two small studies of elite junior handball players aged 17 to 25 found that treadmill sprint-interval sessions raised GH, IGFBP-3, testosterone and the inflammatory marker IL-6, and that a decreasing-distance session produced a larger GH response than an increasing-distance one.[1] The studies measured hormone levels after a session, not height.

Wikipedia reports HIIT modestly reduces subcutaneous fat in healthy people and more in overweight people, and that in teens 8 to 12 weeks of HIIT combined with resistance training reduced waist size and body fat percentage in a 2021 review covering ages 10 to 19. HIIT programmes of a month or more improved cardiovascular fitness in adolescents, and it may be less effective than longer sessions for building muscle or bone mass.

The American College of Sports Medicine recommends consulting a doctor before starting, especially with a history of coronary heart disease, and starting at lower intensity. High-intensity exercise can cause rapid blood pressure spikes, injury risk rises with fatigue and overtraining, and knees, shoulders and ankles are the most commonly injured areas in cited research. Growth-plate injuries such as Salter-Harris fractures can interfere with growth, and Osgood-Schlatter disease involves stress on the tibial growth plate.[3]

No studies found on sprint or HIIT training and final height in adolescents. Related research measures the acute hormone response: GH rises temporarily after maximal sprints in adults and elite junior athletes, with a larger rise after 30-second than after 6-second efforts.[1]

lore.intro: In height-focused forum discussion, sprinting and HIIT are often listed among free ways to support growth during puberty, and in physique discussion HIIT is a staple for fat loss.[2]
